The three core primitives—temporal-spatial imprinting, juxtapositional memory, and sequential impression—are foundational to how cognition encodes external reality. These mechanisms operate through a dual process: passive reception of sensory data followed by structured internal representation. Temporal-spatial imprinting establishes the foundational framework of perception, where the structure of time and space in the environment directly influences neural encoding. Juxtapositional memory builds upon this by reinforcing spatial relationships, enabling complex scene understanding. Sequential impression further enriches cognition by embedding temporal causality. Together, they form a coherent basis for explaining abstract beliefs and concrete idea formation. The failure mode arises when these structures are disrupted—such as in trauma or developmental disorders—where the integrity of these mappings breaks down, leading to fragmented or inaccurate mental models. This suggests that robust cognitive systems must maintain strong alignment between external structure and internal representation.
